theme: Joshua commissioned; Rahab and the spies, faith and the scarlet cord
readingInstruction: Read Joshua 1:1-2:24. Moses is dead, and the people stand on the east bank of the Jordan. Read chapter 1 as a commissioning and chapter 2 as a story about two very different kinds of faith: the nation’s leader gathering courage, and a pagan prostitute in Jericho staking her life on a God she has only heard about.
settingTheScene: Last week you closed the wilderness books with Moses’ death on Mount Nebo. The man who led Israel out of Egypt and received the law at Sinai will not enter the land. Now a new leader steps forward. Joshua has been Moses’ assistant since the early days of the exodus, and he was one of the two spies who trusted God at Kadesh, forty years ago. Israel now stands where their parents stood, at the edge of the promised land. Will this generation believe God where the last one did not? The book of Joshua tells how God keeps the promise he swore to Abraham, and it begins with one command repeated again and again: be strong and courageous.
observation: God speaks to Joshua directly after Moses’ death: “Moses my servant is dead. Now therefore arise, go over this Jordan” (1:2).
The promise is stated in the widest terms, from the wilderness to Lebanon and from the Euphrates to the Great Sea (1:4).
God promises, “Just as I was with Moses, so I will be with you. I will not leave you or forsake you” (1:5).
The command to be “strong and courageous” appears three times in the opening verses (1:6, 7, 9).
Success is tied to meditating on the Book of the Law “day and night” and doing what is written in it (1:8).
Joshua sends two spies secretly from Shittim, and they lodge with Rahab the prostitute (2:1).
Rahab confesses, “The LORD your God, he is God in the heavens above and on the earth beneath” (2:11).
She asks for kindness, and the spies promise protection if she ties a scarlet cord in her window (2:12-21).
interpretation:
The book opens with God’s word to Joshua, and the first thing it does is link the future to the past. “Moses my servant is dead.” The leader has changed, but the promise has not. God does not say, “I will be with you if you prove yourself.” He says, “Just as I was with Moses, I will be with you.” Joshua’s strength will not come from his résumé but from the presence of God. This is why the command to be courageous keeps coming back. Courage in the Bible is never self-confidence. It is the confidence of someone who has been promised that God goes with him.

Notice what makes Joshua strong. It is not a battle plan. It is the book of the law. “This Book of the Law shall not depart from your mouth, but you shall meditate on it day and night.” Joshua is told that success, in the sense of walking wisely and faithfully, comes through Scripture. This is the same pattern as Psalm 1, which you will read soon. The leader of God’s people is first a man under God’s word. The people’s response in the rest of chapter 1 is also striking. They pledge to obey Joshua just as they obeyed Moses, but they add a condition that matters: “Only may the LORD your God be with you, as he was with Moses.” They know that the authority of the leader depends on the presence of God.

Chapter 2 shifts to a very different scene. Joshua sends spies, but the story is not about the spies. It is about a woman in Jericho. Rahab is a Canaanite, a prostitute, and a citizen of a city under God’s judgment. She has no place in the covenant, no history of worship, and no reason to expect mercy. But she has heard what God did at the Red Sea and to the kings east of the Jordan, and she draws a conclusion: “The LORD your God, he is God in the heavens above and on the earth beneath.” It is one of the great confessions of the Old Testament, and it comes from the mouth of someone the reader would never expect.

She acts on that confession at great risk. She hides the spies, misleads the king’s men, and negotiates for the safety of her family. Whatever one concludes about her deception, the text’s focus is her faith, and the New Testament will praise it directly. Hebrews 11:31 says, “By faith Rahab the prostitute did not perish with those who were disobedient.” James 2:25 holds her up as an example of faith that shows itself in works. She is not saved by her works. She is saved because she believed, and her works show it.

The scarlet cord is a quiet image of rescue. Like the blood on the doorposts of the Passover, a visible sign marks the house that will be spared when judgment comes. Christians have long seen in it a picture of the blood of Christ, and even if the text does not say so explicitly, the pattern is clear: judgment will fall on Jericho, and those who take refuge in the way God has provided will be saved. Rahab will become part of Israel. Matthew 1:5 names her in the genealogy of Jesus. A Canaanite prostitute is an ancestor of the Messiah.
connection: The commissioning of Joshua echoes the commissioning of Moses at the burning bush (Exodus 3) and the promise of presence in Deuteronomy 31:6-8. The call to meditate on the law anticipates Psalm 1. Rahab’s confession is the Old Testament’s counterpart to the Gentile faith of the centurion (Matthew 8) and the Canaanite woman (Matthew 15). The scarlet cord recalls the Passover blood in Exodus 12. Rahab is named in Matthew 1:5, Hebrews 11:31, and James 2:25.
application:
First, take courage from the grounds of Joshua’s courage. God does not tell you to be brave because you are capable. He tells you to be brave because he is with you. Think of one situation this week where you feel inadequate, and pray Joshua 1:9 over it.

Second, notice the link between courage and Scripture. If you want to be steady in a shaky season, ask what place God’s word has in your days. What is it shaping in you right now?

Third, let Rahab reshape your idea of who God saves. If you are tempted to think some people are too far gone, remember that God rescued a prostitute from Jericho and put her in the line of Christ. And if you are the one who feels too far gone, she is your encouragement.

Fourth, think about what you have heard of God’s works and how you have responded. Rahab acted on what she heard. What does your life show you believe about him?
prayerPrompts: Tell God about a situation where you feel inadequate, and pray Joshua 1:9 over it.
Ask him to keep his word on your lips and in your mind.
Thank him that he saves those who seem too far gone, as he did Rahab.
